title: Closing Bell: ASIC leaves equity analysts out in cold
full_text:
One of the many changes to the way IPOs are sold in Australia is the way equities research analysts, the ones who truly know their patch and who fund managers trust, have been sidelined by harsher regulation.
The analysts are supposed to be independent, can be a bit unpredictable, and their investment banker colleagues, paid millions to get a deal done for a listing company and/or its owner, can't always trust their research analyst to be on team IPO.
ASIC has progressively clamped down on how investment banks can use their research analysts to win and market IPOs to investors, to the point where research has been largely cut out of the process.
The big change was ASIC's RG264 regulatory guide on sell-side research nearly a decade ago, which altered IPO marketing overnight. Those pre-deal analyst reports got thinner, couldn't put an explicit value on a listing company's shares, and couldn't be fully reviewed by the investment bankers and the listing company prior to publication.
So analysts have largely disappeared from the IPO process. FDC, the biggest IPO in Australia this year, didn't have any pre-deal analyst marketing, while the second-biggest, SkinKandy, had a brief explainer from one of its sponsor brokers (Morgans) that was little more than a copy/paste from the prospectus and didn't touch valuation. GemLife, last year's biggest deal, also had none.
Bankers say these analyst reports are now only necessary for foreign or unusually complex businesses - payments company Cuscal, for example, had an analyst help explain its role in the confusing payments spiderweb and ease concerns about regulatory risk. Maybe it makes sense for Firmus, a likely large and global deal in a new sector with comparable businesses listed offshore.
Investors miss these reports, but the truth is they'd become so bland and there's now so many third-party information sources available that they can live without them.
But ASIC, on a bit of a "Make IPOs and Public Markets Great Again" warpath as shown by its pragmatic approach to SpaceX, has been talking to bankers, lawyers, private equity firms, investors and others in the IPO process, and turned its attention to sell-side research. It's cut that highly prescriptive 42-page RG264 into an eight-page/five principles approach (what Philip Lowe would likely call a "commonsense" approach to guidelines).
Bankers and lawyers will get a copy on Thursday, and it will take an IPO or two under the proposed new guidelines to know how they'll play out. On first reading, the note's much more streamlined which is a good thing, but the substance is largely the same. It is a bit more pragmatic in spirit. ASIC, understandably, wants sell-side analysts to be independent of investment bankers, think differently, be paid separately, and be able to be trusted. Their stance is that these reports are published to help investor clients make decisions about IPOs, not to help get companies listed, which is an important distinction.
So, ASIC has wound back the page count, but not the key restrictions on what analysts can and cannot do: analysts' pre-deal valuations still cannot be seen by bankers/the listing company prior to publication, and analysts are still restricted from talking to listed companies about potential valuations in the pitching process. They are supposed to be independent.
We expect ASIC will get feedback from investment banks and stockbrokers that it could've gone a lot further. AFMA, the banks/brokers/super funds' industry association, told ASIC's capital markets inquiry last year that the sell-side research guidance was "overly prescriptive" and said analysts and their investment banking colleagues could work much more closely without compromising independence. The rest of us don't have to be too cynical to question how that would be possible in the real world.
The bigger issue here is how Australia is placed versus the rest of the world. It is one thing to want to be an IPO puritan when it comes to things like analysts' pre-deal engagement, and another to attract companies to list.
The US is soaking up global investors' dollars, including Australian mums and dads for SpaceX's float, with a different and arguably more lax approach. There are no published pre-deal analyst reports in the US, but analysts have access to a listing company's management and financial model and are heavily involved in valuation discussions with investors in the lead-up to IPO bookbuilds. Reports are published a few weeks after listing (and you could throw a blanket over the views at SpaceX).
So, does it matter? Bankers would point to FDC or SkinKandy's IPOs and say they got away because they were easy-to-understand businesses with decent managements, unaggressive forecasts and inoffensive pricing, rather than anything to do with sell-side research.
But we'd argue it is not filling the IPO bookbuild that ASIC should be thinking about, but rather who's there to buy the stock one week, one month and one year after listing.
It is that secondary market performance, recorded long after bankers have been paid their fees, that is going to do more for the IPO market and public markets long term than just getting an IPO's books covered and the ASX's bell rung by a few faces. And that's where strong (and independent) sell-side research plays a big role.
How do you get good analyst coverage - have analysts involved in pitching for an IPO and cover a stock from pre-listing, or only from the time it is trading? Surely, it's the former - if the bankers can stay out of the way.
